name: French Defense, Steinitz Variation
summary: The Steinitz Variation of the French sees White play 4.e5 and f4 to build a big pawn chain that Black attacks with ...c5 and piece pressure.
intro: The Steinitz Variation arises after 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4 c5 6.Nf3 Nc6 7.Be3, where White grabs space with 4.e5 and props up the d4/e5 chain with f4, while Black counterattacks its base with ...c5, ...Nc6 and pressure on d4.
line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Be3

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The battle is a classic pawn-chain struggle: White's e5- and d4-pawns cramp Black and gain kingside space, so Black attacks the chain at its base with ...c5 and piles up on d4 with ...Nc6, ...Qb6 and ...cxd4. Whoever wins the fight over d4 usually dictates the middlegame.

White's f4 buttresses e5 and hints at a kingside pawn storm, but it also weakens the e6/f7 complex and the e-file over the long term. Black, meanwhile, must free the cramped light-squared bishop and generate queenside counterplay before White's space advantage becomes overwhelming.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: After 7.Be3 Black increases the pressure on d4, typically with ...Qb6 hitting b2 and d4 and often ...cxd4 followed by piece pressure. White must decide whether to maintain the tension, capture on c5, or reroute pieces to defend the crucial d4-point.

Standard plans include ...Be7, ...O-O and a well-timed ...f6 for Black to strike at the e5-spearhead, while White develops with Be2 or Bd3, castles, and looks to the kingside. The struggle over the d4-square and the e5-pawn defines nearly every line.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The variation bears the name of Wilhelm Steinitz, the first official World Champion and a pioneer of positional pawn-chain theory. Fittingly, the line is a textbook illustration of his teachings on space, weak squares and the correct way to attack a pawn chain at its base.

keyIdeas: 4.e5 grabs space and gains a kingside foothold
Black attacks the chain's base with ...c5
The d4-square is the central battleground
f4 later weakens White's e6/f7 and e-file

white: Support the chain with f4 and pieces on d4
Develop with Be2 or Bd3, then castle short
Maintain the e5-spearhead to keep Black cramped
Prepare a kingside pawn advance behind the chain
Reinforce and defend d4 against Black's pressure
black: Pile up on d4 with ...Nc6 and ...Qb6
Challenge e5 with a well-timed ...f6 break
Activate the light-squared bishop with ...b6 or ...a6/...b5
Generate queenside counterplay before White expands
